description: How to evaluate and adopt new tech

screens.body:
Every year brings shiny new frameworks, databases, and AI tools — each claiming to change everything. Most won't. Your job isn't to chase hype; it's to tell signal from noise.

The skill has a name: technology evaluation. It's what separates devs who ship from devs who rewrite their stack every six months.

check.question: The right stance toward new tech:

screens.heading: Hype vs value

screens.body:
Run every new tool through five questions: Does it solve MY problem? Is it mature enough (or am I the guinea pig)? Is the community alive? What's the real total cost? Can I leave if it dies?

That last one — reversibility — is the most underrated. If adopting it is a one-way door, the bar should be sky-high.

options: Can I leave if it dies? (reversibility)
check.question: The most underrated evaluation question:

screens.heading: The five questions
screens.keyPoint: Problem fit, maturity, community, cost, exit.

screens.body:
Never adopt on vibes. Build a proof of concept: a tiny, time-boxed spike — say, one afternoon — solving one real slice of your problem with the new tool.

You'll learn more from four hours of building than forty hours of conference talks. If the spike feels bad, you've spent an afternoon, not a quarter.

options: Rewrite your whole app in it
A tiny time-boxed spike on one real problem
check.question: How do you really evaluate a tool?

screens.heading: Prove it with a spike
screens.keyPoint: Four hours building beats forty hours reading.

screens.body:
The sticker price lies. Total cost includes licenses, learning time, slower onboarding for new devs, and maintenance for years. A 'free' framework that eats a month of learning isn't free.

Flip it too: what's the cost of NOT adopting? Sticking with a dying tool has a price — hiring gets harder, security patches stop.
screens.heading: Count the real cost
screens.keyPoint: Free tools can be expensive. Price the whole picture.

screens.body:
A healthy project shows vital signs: recent releases, answered issues, real companies using it in production, docs that aren't three versions behind.

Check the repo's pulse — last commit date, open issue count, contributor spread. A brilliant tool maintained by one tired person is a risk you should see coming.

options: Recent releases, live issues, real production users
check.question: Signs of a healthy open-source project:

screens.heading: Read the vital signs
screens.keyPoint: Check the repo's pulse before you commit.

screens.body:
Adoption works best as a ladder: try it (spike) → pilot it (one small real feature) → adopt it (team standard for new work) → standardize (migrate old stuff, maybe).

Each rung is a decision point with an exit. You never bet the company on rung one.

options: Try → pilot → adopt → standardize, with exits
check.question: The safe adoption ladder:

screens.heading: Climb the ladder
screens.keyPoint: Every rung has an exit. Never bet it all on rung one.

screens.body:
Saying no is the skill. Say no when the problem is hypothetical, the team would hate maintaining it, or the current tool is fine and boring is good.

Boring technology — the stuff that just works — is underrated. Innovation tokens are limited; spend them where they matter, like SwiftGigs' core flow, not the linter.

options: Never say no to new tech
Say no when the problem is hypothetical or boring works
check.question: When do you say no?

screens.heading: The power of no
screens.keyPoint: Boring tech that works beats exciting tech that might.

screens.body: Thoughtworks Technology Radar (thoughtworks.com/radar). Martin Fowler's bliki on technical strategy (martinfowler.com/bliki).
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The Radar is the industry's shared evaluation ritual.

title: Evaluating New Tech
